title: SaaS stocks: how to analyze SaaS companies
description: SaaS stocks: the subscription model behind software — ARR, churn, gross margin and the Rule of 40. How to analyze SaaS companies, with worked examples.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
SaaS stocks are shares in companies selling software as a subscription — Software as a Service. Instead of a one-time license, contracts renew monthly or annually, and revenue becomes recurring: the same customer pays again without the sales process starting over. That mechanism has given the sector key ratios of its own — ARR, churn and the Rule of 40 — that neither manufacturers nor banks need. AK1A's analysis universe holds the whole span of software economics: from Kambi's 98.9 percent gross margin to Sinch, whose messaging services do not reach 19. This guide works through how to analyze SaaS companies: business model, key ratios, multiple and report reading — education in method, never advice about individual stocks.

## What are SaaS stocks — the subscription is the business

The shift from license to subscription moves revenues in time: a license company books the bulk of the deal when signed; a subscription company spreads it over the contract period as a stream. SaaS companies are therefore measured in ARR — annual recurring revenue, all recurring contracts annualized — rather than reported annual revenue. ARR answers: if nothing happens — no new customers, no cancellations — what does the customer base pay over a year? Growth becomes more visible but more demanding: a one-time deal is booked forever, a subscription can be cancelled next month. The courses [ARR growth](/kurser/v02-arr-tillvaxt) and [the SaaS sector](/kurser/se-01-saassektorn) build on that difference; [the ARR analysis](/blogg/v02-arr-tillvaxt-analys) shows the arithmetic in practice.

## The gross margin reveals the business model

A SaaS company's marginal cost for one more customer is low — same program, same servers, one more user — so the gross margin is the sector's most important fingerprint, and pure software companies sit high. In the universe's raw data (2026-09-15) Kambi reports 98.9 percent, Palantir 84.8, SAP 73.7, Truecaller 73.1 and Microsoft 67.9; at the bottom Sinch at 18.4. The difference is business model, not quality: Sinch relays messaging traffic where the operators' termination fee passes straight through revenues; Kambi's betting platform has a marginal cost near zero. The label "cloud" says nothing about the margin — the business model does. The margin's trend over time is the sector's moat test: holding the margin through price pressure proves the position; being worn down quarter by quarter loses it. Deeper craft: [Gross margin](/kurser/v07-bruttomarginal) and [the gross margin analysis](/blogg/v07-bruttomarginal-analys).

## Churn and NDR — the customer base's own motion

Because revenue recurs, the value lives in the customer base's behavior; two measures capture it. Churn is the share of customers (or revenues) leaving per period. Churn links to relationship length by a simple division: monthly churn of 1 percent gives an average relationship of 1 ÷ 0.01 = 100 months — over eight years; at 2 percent churn it halves to 50. Small churn changes therefore hit valuations hard. NDR — net dollar retention — measures what existing customers pay this year against last year: at 110 percent the base grows ten percent a year without a single new customer — more users, higher tiers, add-on modules. A worked example (invented, round numbers): a customer pays 1,000 kronor per month at 80 percent gross margin — 800 kronor in monthly gross profit. At 2 percent churn the lifetime value becomes 800 × 50 = 40,000 kronor; a customer costing 8,000 to acquire gives the ratio 5:1 — lifetime value against acquisition cost, the sector's classic profitability measure. The mechanisms behind a high NDR — brand and lock-in — are covered in [Brand & customer loyalty](/kurser/v14-varumarke) and [Network effects](/kurser/v15-natverkseffekter).

## Rule of 40 — growth and cash flow in one single number

The sector's summarizing rule of thumb is the Rule of 40: growth rate in percent plus cash flow margin in percent, at least 40 together. The idea: grow fast or generate cash — preferably both. The universe's numbers make it alive: SAP lands at 17.3 + 23.8 = 41.1 — just over. Microsoft, with the sector's heaviest profitability, lands at 19.3 + 5.0 = 24.3 — below the line; companies that size invest the cash instead of collecting it. Palantir shows 44.4 + 35.1 = 79.5 and Sinch 13.1 + 6.1 = 19.2. The rule's point is separation, not judgment: it rewards balance — not maximum growth, not maximum profit. It measures free cash flow, not booked profit — the cash side has its own reading order in [the cash flow analysis](/kurser/km-003-kassaflodesanalysen).

## The multiple — when P/E lacks a denominator

Many SaaS companies are in a phase where profit is small or negative: everything is reinvested in growth. P/E then lacks a denominator, and the sector is valued against revenue — P/S or EV/Sales — the multiple a function of growth, NDR and gross margin. A warning example from the universe: Kambi trades at an EV/EBIT of 197 — not because the company is more expensive, but because EBIT is a fraction of revenue. That is operating leverage made visible: revenues growing through a fixed cost base can collapse profit multiples without the price moving — and vice versa. This is how you count past the trap: compare on EV/Sales or P/S, modulate with the Rule of 40 and churn, and check backwards which growth is priced in — [reverse DCF](/kurser/km-028-reverse-dcf) is the tool. The nuances of multiple choice are in [the P/S ratio](/blogg/ps-tal-nar-ar-det-anvandbart) and [the PEG multiple's weaknesses](/blogg/peg-multipeln-svagheter-2026).

## How to read a SaaS company's report

Five details deserve attention. First, ARR quality: organic growth or acquisitions — and how broad is the customer base ([revenue diversification](/kurser/v03-intaktsdiversifiering))? Second, NDR and churn together: NDR above 100 with rising churn means expansion carries the losses on the way out — an aging customer base in disguise. Third, the gross margin's movement: the moat test again. Fourth, stock-based compensation, SBC: software companies pay partly in shares; the cost shows in dilution rather than the income statement — 2 percent a year becomes 1.02 to the power of 5 ≈ 1.10, ten percent more shares over five years. Fifth, the cash runway: a company burning cash approaches an issue — dilution mechanics worth knowing beforehand ([Emission risk](/kurser/rk-02-emissionrisk)). The reading-order framework: [the quarterly report](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten) and [How to read a Swedish annual report](/blogg/sa-laser-du-en-svensk-arsredovisning).

## The risks — duration, churn and the multiple

The sector's foremost risk lives in time. A SaaS company's cash flows lie far in the future — growth now, cash later — and the farther away, the more rate-sensitive their present value, exactly like long bonds. When rates rise the multiple is pressed down without the business having worsened a single day — the difference between a worse company and a lower price, and the reason to multiply fundamental analysis with valuation. Add churn's cyclical side: in recessions customers review contracts they can cancel — churn rising a few tenths can wipe out a year's growth. Finally competition: software moats are strong but not eternal — new technology changes what customers pay for, and the gross margin shows it earliest.

## The summary

- The subscription model moves revenues in time: ARR — not reported revenue — is the sector's size measure.
- The gross margin reveals the business model: 98.9 percent (Kambi) against 18.4 (Sinch) — "cloud" says nothing, the business does.
- Churn governs the relationship's length (1% → 100 months; 2% → 50); NDR whether the base grows on its own (110% = +10 without new customers).
- The Rule of 40 gathers growth and cash flow: SAP 41.1, Microsoft 24.3, Palantir 79.5 — the rule rewards balance.
- The multiple: when E is small, P/E becomes meaningless (Kambi's EV/EBIT 197) — value against revenue and check what is priced in.
- The biggest risk lives in time: distant cash flows are rate-sensitive, and the multiple can fall without the business worsening.
